extracted.intended_audience: judges, appellate practitioners, and administrative-law scholars focused on rulemaking and judicial review
extracted.subtask_short: judicial review of good cause determinations
extracted.subtask_description: A doctrinal and policy framework for how courts should review agency invocations of the APA's good cause exception to notice-and-comment rulemaking. Focuses on the appropriate standard of review and concrete factors courts should consider when assessing whether good cause exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deference to agency assertions of good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should afford no deference to an agency’s determination that good cause exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard (de novo review) balances public participation, agency flexibility, public safety, and judicial administrability. The article argues that the APA’s text, structure, and objectives make clear that reviewing courts should give no deference to agency assertions of good cause, and that agencies have no interpretive authority over the APA. The D.C. Circuit’s reasoning in Sorenson supports this approach: 'we cannot find that an exception [to the APA] applies simply because the agency says we should.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural issues (including good cause) governed by §706(2)(D) and reviewed de novo
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 706(2)(D) directs courts to 'hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions found to be . . . without observance of procedure required by law,' and that subsection plainly authorizes de novo review of those determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency’s decision to invoke the good cause exception and thus to forgo ordinary procedures is a paradigmatic procedural issue. Courts regularly apply §706(2)(D) to issues like whether a rule is interpretive rather than legislative (which allows skipping notice-and-comment); by parity, good cause invocations should be reviewed under §706(2)(D) rather than under more deferential provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reading §706(2)(A) (arbitrary-and-capricious) to govern routine procedural issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Some circuits review good cause for arbitrariness under §706(2)(A), but doing so risks rendering §706(2)(D) surplusage and is inconsistent with the APA’s structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If courts review all procedural issues under §706(2)(A) on the theory that they were 'not in accordance with law,' §706(2)(D) would be effectively read out of the statute. The proper textual-structural approach gives procedural issues their own treatment under §706(2)(D), supporting de novo review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow construction and demanding inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The good cause exception 'is to be narrowly construed and only reluctantly countenanced.' Courts have described the good cause inquiry as 'meticulous,' 'demanding,' and 'deliberate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These oft-repeated mantras require rigorous scrutiny of good cause assertions and support a de novo standard. Courts should not treat the exception expansively; narrow construction provides an additional basis for rejecting deference to agency claims of good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must make a case of necessity or emergency that is sustainable on review
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress explained the findings supporting good cause assertions must be 'sustainable upon inquiry by a reviewing court' and that a case 'must be made' of necessity or emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies have 'no discretion to disregard [the] terms or the facts' when invoking good cause; courts should probe the facts and require agencies to demonstrate necessity/emergency. Anti-pattern: treating good cause as an 'escape clause' or relying solely on agency assertions without testing the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies lack interpretive authority over the APA; Chevron-style deference is inapposite
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have 'no interpretive authority over the APA' and do not possess specialized expertise regarding the APA akin to the expertise they have with statutes they administer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional justifications for Chevron deference—agency expertise and a background presumption of congressional intent—are not present in the good cause context. Therefore courts should not afford Chevron-style deference to agency claims about compliance with APA procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize agency incentives and risk of self-serving interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: The risk of self-serving agency interpretations is especially pronounced in the good cause context because the only downside for improperly claiming the exception is subsequent invalidation in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies face strong efficiency incentives to claim good cause and have little reason to tread carefully, courts should apply a more exacting (nondeferential) standard of review to counteract agency incentives. Agencies’ litigation risk calculus affects their decision to invoke good cause; courts should be attentive to that dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider congressional design or built-in delay when assessing asserted urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress 'built in' a delay for an agency to specify application (e.g., to pre-enactment actors), that design undercuts an agency's claim of urgency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating whether good cause exists, courts should assess whether Congress provided for a delay or other mechanism that contradicts the agency's urgency rationale. Example: D.C. Circuit in Ross cited Congress’s built-in delay as undermining the Attorney General’s claimed emergency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency delay undermines claims of urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s own delay (e.g., waiting over seven months to publish a rule) can undercut its claim that immediate action was necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of agency action is probative: unexplained or lengthy delays between existence of a problem and promulgation under good cause suggest the emergency/necessity justification is weak. Courts should examine agency behavior and timing as part of the record review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should test agency justifications against the record and make independent determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts examined the agency’s justifications and made independent determinations about whether they were supported by the record; careful testing of arguments against the record is central to de novo review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts should not simply accept proffered rationales at face value but should independently assess evidentiary support. Examples: D.C. Circuit (Ross) and Sixth Circuit (Cain) rejected conclusory speculative harms after testing them against record evidence and congressional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary-and-capricious standard: consider relevant factors and clear error of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard (§706(2)(A)), a court 'must not substitute [its] judgment for that of the agency' but 'must consider whether the decision was based on a consideration of the relevant factors and whether there has been a clear error of judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although this standard has been applied by some circuits to good cause invocations, the Note argues that its deference is doctrinally inappropriate for procedural questions governed by §706(2)(D). Still, courts using this standard will focus on whether the agency considered relevant factors and whether its decision was a clear error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopting de novo review promotes predictability and consistency while preserving flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistently applying a rigorous de novo standard will curtail judicial inconsistencies, help address concerns about contemporary use of the exception, and promote predictability for agencies, litigants, and courts while preserving necessary flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a pragmatic argument for the prescription: changing the standard of review is legally correct, administrable, and less politically fraught than legislative reform. Simplifying the standard can enhance judicial rigor and reduce ad hoc reasoning or inconsistent applications across circuits.
